notes:
Here are the notes on Isaiah 49. I ran out of searches before covering every tradition you asked for, so section 3 is short. The gaps are listed at the end.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Vv. 1–13 overall:** This is usually counted as the second of four "Servant Songs." Precept Austin says the Servant, whom it takes to be the Messiah, is the one speaking in vv. 1–5, and it insists that this is not the nation of Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-49-commentary

**v. 1:** Guzik (Enduring Word) takes the speaker to be the Messiah. He is ordering the coastlands, the distant lands of the Gentiles, to listen to Him. Guzik sees "named Me" fulfilled when Gabriel announced the name Jesus before Mary conceived (Luke 1:31). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ Barnes, quoted by Precept Austin, says "islands" here means distant nations far from Palestine that worshipped idols. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-49-commentary

**v. 2:** The NET note, quoted by Precept Austin, says the Servant's mouth stands for his words. It is compared to a sharp sword because he will speak effectively for God, and he is kept like an arrow in a quiver until the right moment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-49-commentary Guzik thinks the "polished shaft" in the quiver probably refers to Jesus' hidden years of obscurity before His public ministry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 3:** This is the hardest verse. Ellicott says the Servant is not simply the nation; he fulfils its ideal. "Israel" started as one man's name and becomes one person's name again. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49-3.htm Barnes sets out the options. If the verse stood alone it would most naturally mean the Jewish people, but he objects that what is said of this servant does not fit them. Grotius and others applied it to Isaiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/49-3.htm Guzik gives two reasons the Messiah can be called "Israel": He comes from Israel and represents it, and He fulfils the name's meaning, "governed by God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 4:** Guzik puts these words in the Messiah's mouth. Jesus was tempted to think His work was in vain but overcame the temptation by trusting the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ Bible Hub's summary links the verse to the cross: On the cross Jesus looked defeated, echoing the Servant's cry of wasted labor (v 4). The resurrection revealed the true reward. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 5:** MacDonald, quoted by Precept Austin, points out that in verses 5-6 the Servant is distinguished from Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-49-commentary

**v. 6:** The Pulpit Commentary, quoted on Bible Hub, says converting only the Jews would have been "too light" a reward. So God also gave the Servant the gathering of the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49-6.htm Guzik stresses that the Messiah does not just bring salvation; He *is* salvation. He quotes Grogan: "Israel has light but needs restoration, while the Gentiles need both light and salvation." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ GotQuestions notes that Simeon applies the verse to Jesus (Luke 2:32), and Paul applies it to himself and Barnabas (Acts 13:47). https://www.gotquestions.org/Israel-light-to-the-Gentiles.html

**v. 7:** Guzik calls "despised… abhorred by the nation" an important but little-noticed prophecy that the Messiah would be rejected, both by people generally and by Israel. In the end kings will honour Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 8:** Guzik says Jesus *is* the covenant, not just the one who brings it. He applies "I will help You" especially to the cross and the hope of resurrection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ Ellicott links "covenant" to Jeremiah 31:31 and the Last Supper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/49-8.htm Paul quotes this verse in 2 Corinthians 6:2. Kruse says that in their original context these words are addressed to the Servant of the Lord and applied to the time of Israel's release from exile in Babylon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-6-commentary

**v. 9:** Guzik gives examples of Jesus freeing prisoners: the demon-possessed, the sick, those in bondage to sin and the law. He also cites Ephesians 4:8 for the righteous dead being released. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ Bible Hub gives the Cyrus Cylinder, which records Cyrus sending exiles home, as background for "Come out." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 10:** Guzik sees two layers. Near at hand, God provides for the exiles coming home from Babylon. In the larger sense, He provides for people returning to Him in the last days. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ The BSB footnote says Revelation 7:16 quotes this verse. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 11:** Guzik, drawing on Redpath, notes the wording "*My* mountains." The obstacles still belong to God and have a loving purpose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 12:** The BSB footnote explains that "Aswan," in southern Egypt, comes from the Dead Sea Scrolls. The standard Hebrew text (MT) reads "Sinim." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm Guzik gives the views: Aswan, China, or (Grogan) a deliberately vague name meaning God will gather people even from unmapped places. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 13:** Guzik: the LORD calls on creation itself to join the praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 14:** Guzik: "Zion" stands for God's people. In exile they wonder whether God really cares, and the rest of chapters 49–50 answers them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**v. 15:** Guzik: the LORD's love for His people is greater than a mother's for her nursing child. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ Young, quoted by Precept Austin, calls this one of the strongest, if not the strongest expression of God's love in the Old Testament. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60569/

**v. 16:** Ellicott says the picture comes from tattooing, a bold human image for God. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49-16.htm Barnes lists the theories (a reminder sign, a tattoo, an architect's plan) and prefers Lowth's tattoo view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/49-16.htm Calvin says God has no body, but Scripture stoops to our weakness to show how strongly He loves us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-16.html Guzik sees the verse fulfilled in Jesus' nail-scarred hands. Matthew Henry notes only that "some" apply it that way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-16.html Gill says the "walls" are the walls of God's church, not Jerusalem's walls waiting to be rebuilt. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/isaiah/49-16.html Ligonier's devotional says the walls are Jerusalem's broken walls during the exile. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/engraved-on-gods-hands

**v. 17:** The BSB footnote says "builders" comes from the Dead Sea Scrolls; the MT reads "your sons." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 18:** Guzik: the exiles brought home will be Zion's ornament, which shows God's faithfulness about her future. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/

**vv. 19–21:** Bible Hub's summary: the once-empty land overflows. When Zion asks who bore these children, the implied answer is that the LORD did. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 22:** I found only Bible Hub's summary: the LORD raises His banner, and Gentile kings and queens carry Israel's children. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 23:** Barnes: kings would protect the church by their laws and support it with their influence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/49-23.htm Matthew Henry: partly fulfilled after the return from exile, and later in rulers such as Constantine and Helena. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-23.html Poole explains "lick the dust" as Eastern bowing so low the face touches the ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/49-23.htm

**vv. 24–25:** The Bridgeway Bible Commentary says some exiles doubted they could be freed, because Babylon seemed unbeatable. God answers that He can do it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-23.html Guzik: Babylon took Zion captive, but even Babylon's captives will be taken back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ The BSB footnote says "tyrant" in v. 24 follows the Dead Sea Scrolls, Syriac and Vulgate; the MT reads "of the righteous." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**v. 26:** I found only Bible Hub's summary: the oppressors are crushed, and everyone learns that the LORD is Israel's Saviour and Redeemer. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

---

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 3, who the Servant is:**
- **Calvin (Reformed)** says the verse must not be limited to the person of Christ, and ought not to be referred to Israel alone. To him "Israel" here includes the Church, which was given God's word to spread through the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-3.html On v. 8 he makes a similar move: Paul applies the verse to the whole Church, but "covenant" fits Christ alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-8.html
- **Guzik (enduringword.com, on your Pentecostal/charismatic list) and MacDonald (via Precept Austin)** read the verse as about Christ alone, not the nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-49-commentary

**vv. 5–8, ethnic Israel and the future:**
- **Guzik** says v. 5 shows that ethnic Israel still has a place in God's plan, to be fulfilled when "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-49/
- **MacArthur (Baptist, Grace to You)**, quoted by Precept Austin, says Israel will finally do its mission to the nations very effectively in the tribulation after the conversion of the 144,000 witnesses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-49-commentary
- **Constable** reads v. 8 this way: the day of salvation began at the cross, God has not yet given the land back to Israel, and the day will reach its high point in a future millennium (a 1,000-year reign of Christ). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-8.html
- **Ellicott (older Anglican)**, by contrast, says the prophet may have expected a literal fulfilment, but readers who see the prophecy fulfilled look to a spiritual inheritance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/49-8.htm

**v. 8 and 2 Cor 6:2, the "day of salvation":**
- **Calvin** stresses that salvation comes from God's free favour alone. He reasons that because a particular day is named, a free offer of salvation is not made every day. https://ccel.org/study/2_Corinthians_6:2
- **Adam Clarke**, whom StudyLight labels Wesleyan/Methodist and Arminian, reads the verse as predicting the days of the Messiah and the grace then given. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/6-2.html

**v. 23, kings as "nursing fathers":**
- **Calvin** uses the verse to reject the idea that kings cannot be Christians unless they give up their office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-23.html
- **Henry** says the promise is fulfilled whenever religious rulers hold power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-23.html
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel)** reads it as Israel's glorious future, when the kings of the earth come to honour her. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/49-23.html

---

## 3. Other views

- **Older critical scholarship:** Barnes reports that Rosenmüller took the Servant to be the Jewish nation. Gesenius doubted that the word "Israel" in v. 3 is original. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-49.html
- **Septuagint (Greek Old Testament):** In v. 6 it reads differently, including "covenant of a race." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49-6.htm
- **Popular modern teaching:** Bible Hub's chapter notes say the ingathering of vv. 11–12 is still happening as Jewish communities return to the land today. They compare vv. 22–23 to Persia's decrees, the Balfour Declaration (1917) and current diplomacy. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/49.htm

**Not found:** Catholic and Orthodox readings (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), modern scholarship from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org beyond the NET note above, Lutheran sources, and anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. I also found no detailed comment on vv. 19–22 or v. 26 beyond Bible Hub's summary. Another round of research would be needed to fill these gaps.
